clinicalPearls: Radiographic hallmark is marked flaring and undermodelling of the metaphyses, producing the classic Erlenmeyer-flask deformity, most obvious at the distal femur
In contrast to craniometaphyseal dysplasia, the skull and facial bones are relatively spared, and cranial-nerve compression is not a prominent feature
Caused by autosomal recessive loss-of-function variants in SFRP4, a secreted WNT antagonist important for bone modelling
The widened metaphyses have thin cortices, so bone can be fragile and fractures may occur despite the expanded appearance
Clinical features are often mild and may include genu valgum, mild limb deformity and joint discomfort, with many individuals otherwise well
Dental problems and mild vertebral changes can occur, but intelligence and life expectancy are typically normal
Management is orthopaedic and supportive, addressing limb deformity and fractures, since the disorder is comparatively benign
reference.pathophysiology: Pyle disease results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SFRP4, which encodes a secreted frizzled-related protein that normally antagonises WNT signalling and helps regulate the modelling of bone during growth. Loss of this antagonist disturbs the coordinated resorption and shaping that narrows the metaphysis into the diaphysis, so the metaphyses remain broad and undermodelled, giving the Erlenmeyer-flask appearance. The expanded metaphyseal bone has thinned cortices, accounting for a degree of fragility despite the bulky radiographic appearance. Because the skull is relatively spared compared with the craniotubular dysplasias, the disorder lacks the severe cranial-nerve and craniofacial complications seen in those conditions.
additionalDifferentials: Osteopetrosis (which can also cause an Erlenmeyer-flask deformity)
Gaucher disease with metaphyseal remodelling failure
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating the Erlenmeyer-flask metaphyseal flaring, especially at the knees
Skeletal survey to assess the extent of metaphyseal undermodelling and cortical thinning
Skull imaging to confirm relative sparing and distinguish from craniometaphyseal dysplasia
Assessment of limb alignment for genu valgum and deformity
SFRP4 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Dental evaluation where dental anomalies are present
redFlags: Fractures through thinned metaphyseal cortices despite the expanded bone
Progressive limb deformity impairing function and requiring orthopaedic correction
Atypical skull involvement or cranial-nerve symptoms prompting reconsideration towards craniometaphyseal dysplasia
Features suggesting an alternative marrow-storage or sclerosing disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good, with normal intelligence and life expectancy; morbidity relates mainly to limb deformity and occasional fractures rather than the neurological complications of the craniotubular dysplasias.
pitfalls: Confusing Pyle disease with craniometaphyseal dysplasia, which has prominent skull involvement and cranial-nerve compression
Assuming the bulky metaphyses are strong when the thin cortices predispose to fracture
Attributing an Erlenmeyer-flask deformity solely to Pyle disease without considering osteopetrosis or Gaucher disease
Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance when counselling families
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: No disease-specific treatment exists; care is supportive because most individuals are only mildly affected
Refer for orthopaedic correction of genu valgum and limb deformity, with corrective osteotomy where alignment is significantly disturbed
Manage fractures with awareness that the expanded metaphyses have thin, fragile cortices
Provide simple analgesia and physiotherapy for joint discomfort
Arrange dental evaluation where dental anomalies are present
Monitor limb alignment and growth periodically during childhood
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SFRP4 disorder
